english_translation: Traditional homesteads were built with wooden poles and thatched with grass rather than metal sheets.

dialogue.shona: Misha yechinyakare yaivakwa nembariro ichipwigirwa nehuswa kwete marata.
dialogue.english: Traditional homesteads were built with wooden poles and thatched with grass rather than metal sheets.
dialogue.literal_gloss: Misha [misha] • yechinyakare [yechinyakare] • yaivakwa [yaivakwa] • nembariro [and / with mbariro] • ichipwigirwa [ichipwigirwa] • nehuswa [and / with huswa] • kwete [kwete] • marata [plural rata]

grammar_notes.title: Joining Words with 'ne-' ('and / with') in 'nembariro'
grammar_notes.content: Look closely at 'nembariro'. In Shona, the word for 'and' or 'with' between nouns is not a separate word—instead, the prefix 'ne-' (or 'na-' before people's names) is written attached directly to the second noun! For example, 'ne-' + 'mbariro' forms 'nembariro'. You will see this everywhere in daily speech: 'sadza nemuriwo' ('sadza and vegetables'), 'nesimba' ('with strength'), and 'nekukasira' ('with haste / quickly').
grammar_notes.rule: ne- + Noun = and / with [Noun] (written as a single word, e.g., sadza nemuriwo = sadza and vegetables)

grammar_notes.title: How Shona Sentences Fit Together (Subject + Tense + Verb)
grammar_notes.content: In 'Misha yechinyakare yaivakwa nembariro ichipwigirwa nehuswa kwete marat...', notice how a single Shona verb word packs together who is doing the action (the subject prefix), when it happens (the tense marker), and the action itself (the verb stem). Once you recognize the building blocks at the start of the verb—like 'ndi-' (I), 'u-' (you), 'ti-' (we), or 'va-' (they)—you can immediately spot the subject even when no separate pronoun word is used!
grammar_notes.rule: [Who (Subject Prefix)] + [When (Tense Marker)] + [Action (Verb Root)] -> e.g., ti- (we) + -cha- (will) + -svika (arrive) = tichasvika

grammar_notes.title: Describing Nouns: Word Order in Shona
grammar_notes.content: In English, descriptive words like adjectives, possessives ('my', 'our'), demonstratives ('this', 'that'), and numbers come BEFORE the noun ('this big house', 'my two books'). In Shona, the noun always comes FIRST, and all descriptive words follow right after it! For example: 'nyama iyi' ('this meat'), 'mwana uyu' ('this child'), 'goho guru' ('a big harvest'), and 'makomo marefu' ('tall mountains').
grammar_notes.rule: Noun FIRST + Descriptor SECOND -> mota iyi (this car), mabhuku edu (our books), makomo marefu (tall mountains)

cultural_notes.title: Everyday Communication, Politeness & Community Life
cultural_notes.content: In everyday Shona conversation (as in 'Traditional homesteads were built with wooden poles and thatched with grass rath...'), speakers place a strong emphasis on politeness, patience, and consideration for others around them—whether asking for help ('ndinokumbirawo undibatsire'), speaking quietly when someone is resting or studying, or sharing news with family at the end of the day.

active_exercises.prompt: How do you say 'two women and four men' in Shona?
active_exercises.explanation: 'Vakadzi vaviri' = 'two women' (-viri = 2) and 'nevarume vana' = 'and four men' (-na = 4).
